stance_basis: opens letter explicitly opposing motorized vehicle trails in national forests and arguing ORVs should not be considered an important recreational asset
summary: Indiana Sassafras Audubon, a young conservation organization based in Nashville, Indiana, submitted a formal comment letter opposing the establishment of motorized vehicle trails in national forests, specifically referencing the Hoosier National Forest proposal. The organization argued that ORV use is economically unjustified, harmful to wildlife and non-motorized users, incompatible with sound land management, and primarily benefits a narrow commercial interest (motorcycle manufacturers and sellers) at taxpayer expense. They also raised concerns about noise pollution, public health, displacement of wildlife, and the adverse effects on hikers and future generations.
complaint_summary: Indiana Sassafras Audubon opposes ORV trail establishment in national forests, arguing the Hoosier National Forest proposal disproportionately benefits motorcycle industry interests at taxpayer expense, harms wildlife and non-motorized users, raises public health and noise concerns, and is incompatible with sound land management for future generations.

statement.text:
Indiana Sassafras Audubon opposes the establishment of motorized vehicle trails in national forests. We feel there is no reason that national forests have to consider ORVs as an important recreational asset in the forest land.
Our opinions are based on close observation of the controversy in our own National Hoosier Forest, participation at a hike conducted by the Forest Service on July 15, 1972 (see enclosed newspaper clipping) in the Hickory Ridge Area near Monroe Reservoir, and the Draft Environmental Analysis, proposed Off Road Vehicle Policy, Hoosier National Forest (2350) of July 14, 1972 as supplied to this society by U.S. Department of Agriculture Forest Service.
Out of app. 160,000 acres of land in National Hoosier Forest the Forest Service proposes to open app. 99,000 acres to ORV trail use, while only 62,000 acres would remain closed. The initial cost for these trails would be anywhere between 0500,000.00 to 01,000,000.00 with the maintenance cost 050,000.00 per year and administrative cost 025,000.00 to 050,000.00 per year. This would benefit with the exception of a few independent users, almost exclusively the app. 1000 nembers of the Indiana Motorcycle Association. The beneficiaries (the major interest group manipulating the INA for opening up the national forest to ORV use) are the manufacturers and sellers of motorcycles—for the most part Japanese made.

The other adverse effect given in DES 72-62 p.28 is 2) the economies of areas near department lands were ORV use takes place. To this I would like to present the following observation made at the Brown County State Park on the State level. The park is at present overused by campers, while private camp grounds, abundant in Brown County (and one of the only means of income in an area, that has to rely on the tourist dollar) are having a hard time competing with the lower prices inside the park area. If the park were closed to campers the economy of the area would go up, the cost would be taken off the taxpayer's shoulder who has to pay for the overuse by excessive maintenance cost and would place it onto the camper-user. The same would hold true for the ORV industry. Tourism is very definitely an industry and should be placed entirely into the private sector and financed by those who engage in the different recreational uses.
There are many other perfectly legitimate recreational uses beginning with golf, swinning, baseball etc. that are not financed out of federal funds and accomplated on public lands as 0 % users are desiring in the case of establishing and maintaining expansive trails.

Page 4 of DES 72-62 discusses use criteria. What constitutes "minimal damage". Should it be compared to "normal wear", i.e. the use of forest land by wildlife, by the human foot. Does a tire of a car or motorcycle still constitute normal wear? P.5 d) what does "exessive" damage mean?
Page 8: "The biota of these lands comprise a resource recognized as significant in its contribution to sustaining mankind." In which way is ORV use here compatible at all. How about the "unimpaired" use for the enjoyment of future generations. Will an experiment in "controlled" use of public lands by ORVs irreversibly damage much of the lands for the general public of tomorrow.
On pages 13 and 14 DES 72-62 deals with the potential damage of ORV use upon public lands. The physical as well as biologic impacts clearly demonstrate incompatibility of this "recreation" and the place designated for it. The only positive impact cited (p.17) is "an economic boost for the general market", but this boost is 1) for the temporary benefit of individuals or companies and not for the general public. The DEA Hoosier National Forest states on p.2, sec. B):
"In the administration of the Forest Reserves, it must be clearly borne in mind that all land is to be devoted to the most productive use for the permanent good of the whole people and not for the temporary benefit of individuals or companies ..."
The effect upon wildlife is discussed in DES 72-62 on pays 15. In an area like that of National Hoosier Porest surrounded by a rapidly growing population, increasing in density and urban are well the displacement of unimals is significant without farther displacement of wildlife inside National Possier Forest. In aroun County more dear and other animals have been killed in the past few years then ever before, not because there is areater abuncate, but because of a large increase in construction the animals were driven out of their normal habitat. Two years ago deer around our home were frequent, this year there has been none.
How about the rights of the public lands themselves as discussed on page 22 of DES. Are "sound land management" and ORV use compatible at all. How about rallies, meets, endurance contests? Should activities like these not be taking place in and area, built and maintained for this particular purpose by the industry to supplyes. May does the taxpayer have to finance them.

Public Health: p27 cites that accidents involving use of ORVs are on the increase. The noise levels involved, according to National Hoosier Forest DEA p.ll, are such that they will damage even the operator of the ORV and the problem will be compounded by ORV users running in groups. The noise involved will definitely interfere with the enjoyment of those who are out to walk and walking is a very healthy leisure activity. Many hikers are at present discouraged by interference with minibiles and disillusion with this sport is reported by our members.
The existence of ORV trails will have an adverse effect upon non-ORV users. It will hasten to make our nation one of people who do not know how to use legs. It will be even more consequential at a time when many young people are just beginning to discover the joy of backpacking and going out into nature.
A 7.5 billion Federal Aid Highway Act of 1972 was reported to Public Works Committee on July 21, 1972. This would include funds for an increased safety program, improved emergency medical care for victims of accidents (will these funds help victims of ORV use accidents). But most of all the proposal would allow the use of Highway Trust funds money for mass transportation.
At a time when the need for a mass transportation system has become quite clear for many reasons, one of which is cutting down on air pollution, the internal combustion engine will be invading our public lands. Ford Motor Company was forced into complying with the standards set by EPA for emission control. But Japanese make bicycles will be polluting those parts of our public lands were people would like to go for peace and solitude and to get away from the traffic and noises of the city. Encouragement of this industry would result from opening the lands; what appears "controllable" at the present will become a nightware. The graneral public and the future generations will pay for it - later.
Indiana Presaires Audubon Society is a young organization. It was founded in December 1970 and has since then grown to a membership of a region. It is growing at a rapid rate. New chapters are a right; up everywhere and National Audubon is growing at a rate of 3000-4000 members a month. We feel these are give heart numbers of people, who have admowledged their interdependence with nature, and who look for protection to the Federal and State Governments.
